common_name: Princess of Hanover Rex Begonia (Spiral Silver-Olive Foliage)

planting.note: Propagate from rhizome divisions or leaf-wedge cuttings taken in spring, rooting under high humidity at 70-75°F.

directions: A sport of the venerable Victorian-era 'Queen of Hanover', this heirloom rex begonia produces tightly spiraled leaves in olive-green washed with metallic silver, the coiled centers deepening to near-black and the undersides flushed dark red. Grow in bright, indirect light with steady warmth and high humidity, since the papery leaves scorch in direct sun and stall in cold drafts. Water only when the top inch of the rhizome's shallow, well-drained mix has dried, as rex begonia rhizomes rot quickly in soggy soil. Its tighter, more compact spiral distinguishes it from larger-leaved spiral cultivars like Escargot.

common_name: Baby Bunny Bellies Speedy Jenny (Fuzzy Green Trailing Spiderwort)

planting.note: Root 3-4 inch stem-tip cuttings directly in moist potting mix or water; nodes root within a week or two under warm, bright conditions.

directions: Distinct from the smooth-leaved wandering jews commonly grown, this species and its 'Baby Bunny Bellies' selection carry small, thick, oval leaves densely covered in soft white hairs that give the foliage a velvety, almost furry texture, with rosy-purple undersides showing through on new growth. Grow in bright indirect to gentle direct light, which intensifies the pink blush and keeps the trailing stems compact rather than stretched. Let the top of the mix dry between waterings, since the fuzzy foliage is prone to rot if water sits on the leaves or the soil stays wet. Its fine pubescence and diminutive, rounded leaves separate it clearly from zebrina, fluminensis, and pallida selections already in cultivation.

common_name: Shivereana Variegated Rubber Plant (Marbled Cream-Green Leaves)

planting.note: Air-layer or root single-node stem cuttings with the sap allowed to callus for a few hours first; provide bottom heat and a humidity tent for faster rooting.

directions: One of the earliest variegated rubber tree selections, Shivereana bears thick, leathery leaves in pale cream to sage-green mottled with irregular dark green blotches, a softer, marbled pattern rather than the crisp pink-edged variegation of Tineke or the solid burgundy of Burgundy. Give it the brightest indoor light available short of direct midday sun, since low light causes the pale sectors to fade back toward plain green. Allow the top few inches of mix to dry before watering thoroughly, and wipe the broad leaves occasionally to keep pores clear of dust. Older leaves are shed from the base as the plant grows taller, eventually forming a small, leggy tree that benefits from occasional pruning to encourage branching.

common_name: Moon Valley Friendship Plant (Deeply Quilted Bronze-Green Foliage)

planting.note: Root 2-3 inch stem-tip cuttings in moist mix under high humidity at 70-75°F; pinch regularly once established to keep growth dense.

directions: The most widely sold selection of friendship plant, Moon Valley carries heavily crinkled, crater-like leaves in chartreuse to bronze-green with deeply sunken purple veins, a more pronounced 'moonscape' texture and brighter coloring than the plain species or the silvery, charcoal-veined Norfolk cultivar. Grow in bright indirect light with elevated humidity, since dry indoor air quickly browns the thin, puckered leaf edges. Keep the humus-rich mix evenly moist but never waterlogged, and pinch growing tips regularly to prevent the mounding stems from sprawling and going bare at the base. Refresh plants from cuttings every year or two, as older stems become woody and lose their compact habit.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension — Pilea involucrata
